previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis and neurogenic bladder managed with a suprapubic catheter, was admitted with a catheter-associated urinary tract infection presenting with fever, hand weakness, and foul-smelling urine. He was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics due to a history of multidrug-resistant organisms. Initial urine culture showed mixed flora suggestive of contamination, prompting a CT scan which ruled out a colovesical fistula. The infection was ultimately attributed to vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus sensitive to ampicillin, and he completed a 12-day course of piperacillin-tazobactam via a PICC line. During admission, he developed transient somnolence and hypercarbia, prompting evaluation for seizure and stroke; EEG and CT head were normal, and the episode resolved after discontinuing ramelteon. He also received IV iron for iron deficiency anemia. He improved clinically, with normalization of labs and resolution of symptoms, and was discharged home with follow-up arranged in neurology, urology, and infectious disease.
